newsitem.title: PERU: After siege boost, Peru's Fujimori drops in poll.
newsitem.headline: After siege boost, Peru's Fujimori drops in poll.

text.p: After a surge on the Lima hostage crisis, Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's popularity has renewed its slide on disapproval of his re-election drive and pocketbook-related worries, a poll said on Sunday.

A survey by polling firm Imasen, published in local newspapers, showed Fujimori's popularity rating had fallen to 45.2 percent in early February after halting a downward trend and rising to 50.3 percent in late December.
His disapproval rating, meanwhile, climbed to 49.4 percent versus 44.5 percent in the earlier survey, Imasen said.

The poll of 405 people in metropolitan Lima also showed 62.5 percent said they would not vote for Fujimori if he stands for re-election in 2000 while 29.9 percent said they would. No margin of error for the survey was given.

Fujimori, a son of Japanese immigrants who has enjoyed strong public support for his virtual defeat of leftist rebels and for slashing inflation, is now in his second five-year term. He was first elected in 1990.

The Dec. 17 takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels has presented Fujimori with the worst crisis of his turbulent six-year period in office.
According to Imasen, 64.2 percent said they believe Fujimori has a strategy for resolving the hostage crisis and freeing the 72 captives.

Imasen director Giovanna Penaflor was quoted by financial daily Gestion as saying that people were turning their attention from the 54-day hostage crisis to other issues closer to home and to the wallet.

"The reading of these figures is that, with the prolonging of the hostage crisis, the central axes always used to measure presidential support are being rediscovered: jobs, economic situation, the re-election effort, etc," she told financial daily Gestion.

The polls also found that 95.1 percent favour the Red Cross' role during the crisis while 87.9 percent back the work of Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a mediator in the 7-week-old hostage drama.
